title: Why do packed cafes still close?
subtitle: A case study of India's cafe boom: Third Wave, Cafe Coffee Day, Starbucks, Barista, the hype cafes and the tier-2 cities.

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.markdown:
**Why do packed cafes still close, and why are the next great ones opening in Lucknow?**

*A reel can fill your cafe once. Only the second visit pays the rent.*

Audience: founders, operators, case competitors · About 22 minutes · Topics: Consumer & Retail, Growth Strategy, Pricing, Competitive Advantage · Companion to *The cafe owner's toolkit*

A **case study** is the story of what a real company did, why it worked or failed, and what we can learn from it. Here we look at India's cafe boom through the cafes that grew, the ones that shrank, and the new map forming outside the metros. The frameworks behind each lesson are explained in the toolkit booklet; this booklet is the evidence.

> **Download the 10-slide deck:** [Why do packed cafes still close? deck (PowerPoint)](content/decks/why-packed-cafes-close-deck.pptx)

chapters.title: The bucket with no bottom
chapters.markdown:
Think of a cafe as a bucket. Marketing pours guests in: a reel, an influencer, a launch offer. Repeat visits are the bottom of the bucket, the part that holds them. A bucket with no bottom can be filled every day and still always be empty, and that is exactly how a packed cafe goes out of business.

India's cafe boom is real. The country had 5,339 branded coffee shops in 2025, 600 more than a year earlier, and 57% of cafe-goers visit at least once a week ([World Coffee Portal](https://www.worldcoffeeportal.com/news/india-a-branded-coffee-shop-market-brimming-with-potential), 2025). Thus demand is not the problem. The problem is that most new cafes are built to win the first visit, while the rent is paid by the second, the third and the fiftieth. Hence the cafes that last are the ones that plan for repeat guests before they plan the launch.

The story has a second half. Outside the six big metros, rents are a fraction of Bengaluru's or Delhi's, guests come for conversation rather than photos, and chains such as Barista now say their smaller-city cafes earn more than their metro ones ([Restaurant India](https://www.restaurantindia.in/news/restaurant-india-news-barista-coffee-targets-800-900-stores-by-2030-eyes-tier-ii-iii-towns-for.n15095), 2026). So the same lesson, build for the second visit, plays out on two very different maps.

**Three takeaways**

**The mechanism:** first visits are cheap to win and return visits pay the bills. e.g. About 85 of every 100 first-time restaurant guests never come back ([Bloom Intelligence](https://bloomintelligence.com/blog/first-time-restaurant-guests-return-rate/), 2026), hence a launch crowd is mostly a one-time crowd.

**The hard part:** rent is fixed, footfall is not. A cafe on a famous street pays the same rent on a quiet Tuesday as on a viral Saturday, thus a slow month hurts far more than a busy one helps.

**The twist:** the smaller market can be the safer bet. A good high street in Lucknow or Kochi needs about a third of the daily customers that Indiranagar does to carry its rent, hence the next great cafes may open far from the reels.

> *"A reel can fill your cafe once. Only your coffee can fill it twice."*

chapters.title: The four tests every cafe faces
chapters.markdown:
A **survival test** here means a question a cafe must answer correctly to stay open past its second year. Every cafe in this booklet, from a 600 sq ft Bandra cafe to Tata Starbucks, faced the same four. We take them in the order a founder meets them.

**Test 1, can the street carry the rent?** The rule of thumb is to keep rent under 20% of revenue ([Restaurant India](https://www.restaurantindia.in/article/cafe-business-in-india-setup-cost-profit-margins-what-nobody-tells-you.16054), 2026). This sounds simple, but it quietly sets our sales target before we sell a single cup. e.g. A 1,000 sq ft cafe on Indiranagar's 100 Feet Road pays Rs 375 per sq ft a month ([Cushman & Wakefield](https://assets.cushmanwakefield.com/-/media/cw/marketbeat-pdfs/2026/q3/apac-and-gc/bengaluru-retail-q3-2026.pdf?rev=50b06e88da194a1993c7f4776a06ec74), Q3 2026), so it needs about 179 bills a day at Rs 350 each just to keep rent at 20%. Hence the famous street is often the most expensive way to be busy.

**Test 2, does the cafe do one job well?** Guests don't buy coffee; they hire a place to meet, to work or to get a quick daily fix. A cafe that tries to be all three ends up with the wrong seats, the wrong hours and the wrong menu for everyone. e.g. Chaayos built its 200+ cafes around the daily chai habit and reached an 11.9% EBITDA margin in FY25 ([Entrackr](https://entrackr.com/fintrackr/chaayos-crosses-rs-300-cr-revenue-in-fy25-ebitda-jumps-65x-11088950), 2025), thus a narrow job can be a strong business.

**Test 3, do guests come back?** This is the test most new cafes fail, because it shows up only after the launch excitement fades. If a cafe needs 3,300 bills a month and a regular visits four times, it needs about 825 regulars. At the benchmark rate of 3 regulars per 100 first-time guests, finding them takes about 27,500 first visits. A strong launch reel might bring 3,000. Hence hype can fill the cafe for a month but cannot carry it for a year.

**Test 4, did the first cafe prove itself before the next one opened?** Growth multiplies whatever we have, good or bad. A chain that opens ten cafes before the first is profitable has ten problems instead of one, and if the growth is funded with debt, the problem can become fatal. Thus the order matters: prove, then grow.

The four tests separate two kinds of cafe:

| Choice | Hype-led cafe | Habit-led cafe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where the money goes first | Interiors and launch reels | Coffee, staff training, a way to capture each first visit |
| Location | The famous street | The street the revenue can carry |
| Menu | Large, built for photos | Small, built around one job |
| First visit | A crowd, often overwhelmed | Name and number taken, follow-up within 30 days |
| Month six | Queue gone, rent unchanged | Regulars carry the weekday |

The frameworks behind each test, rent-to-revenue, jobs to be done, the retention funnel and the Ansoff matrix, are explained step by step in *The cafe owner's toolkit*.

chapters.title: Third Wave Coffee and the big names
chapters.markdown:
### Context

Third Wave Coffee is a specialty cafe chain founded in Bengaluru in 2015. It became the poster child of the metro cafe boom: good beans, bright interiors and a store opening every few weeks. By FY24 it had grown fast, but the stores weren't paying for themselves. The case is useful because it is a large, well-funded version of the exact mistake small cafes make, and because it shows the way out.

### Key metrics

| Metric | Figure | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Net loss, FY24 | Rs 110 crore, more than double the year before | [IBTimes](https://www.ibtimes.co.in/third-wave-coffees-net-losses-grow-over-2-times-rs-110-crore-fy24-875041) |
| Stores losing money, FY24 | About 70% | [The Ken](https://the-ken.com/story/inside-third-wave-coffees-unending-reinvention/) |
| Revenue and loss, FY25 | Rs 285 crore revenue; loss cut to Rs 94 crore | The Ken |
| Stores EBITDA positive after the reset | Over 90% at store level | The Ken |

### What happened, in three phases

**Phase 1, the dash (2015 to FY24).** Third Wave raised money and opened cafes quickly across metros. Revenue rose every year, but so did the loss, and [World Coffee Portal](https://www.worldcoffeeportal.com/news/third-wave-coffee-sees-full-year-sales-surge-but-losses-widen-amid-dash-for-growth/) (2024) put it down to staffing, rent and raw materials. In the language of Chapter 2, it was failing Test 4: each new store added to the loss instead of the profit. Hence, by FY24, about seven in ten stores were losing money.

**Phase 2, the reset (FY24 to FY25).** The company brought in Rajat Luthra, formerly head of KFC India, as CEO. Instead of opening more, it went store by store: fixing rent, staffing and menus, and closing what could not be fixed. The loss fell from Rs 110 crore to Rs 94 crore while revenue grew to Rs 285 crore. Thus the same brand, with the same coffee, started to work once each store was made to pay.

**Phase 3, growth again, this time outside metros (FY26).** With more than 90% of stores EBITDA positive, Third Wave started opening again, and its 250th cafe opened in Lucknow, with a target of 320 by FY27 ([Restaurant India](https://www.restaurantindia.in/news/third-wave-coffee-opens-250th-caf-in-lucknow-targets-320-outlets-by-fy27.n17309), 2026). The order is the lesson: prove, then grow.

### The same story at other sizes

**Cafe Coffee Day** went from 1,752 cafes in FY19 to 469 in FY23 under group debt of Rs 7,214 crore ([Financial Express via Third Eyesight](https://www.thirdeyesight.in/?p=6053), 2023). Guests did not stop drinking coffee; the cafes were funded faster than they could repay. Hence debt turned a growth problem into a survival problem.

**Tata Starbucks** grew revenue 5% to Rs 1,277 crore in FY25, while its loss widened to Rs 135.7 crore ([Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/corporate/tata-starbucks-fy25-losses-widen-to-rs-1357-crore-revenue-rises-5-to-rs-1277-crore), 2025). Tata has since asked for smaller, cheaper stores before it puts in more capital ([Outlook Business](https://www.outlookbusiness.com/corporate/starbucks-asked-to-cut-costs-in-india-as-tatas-halt-fresh-investments)). Thus even the world's biggest coffee brand is being pushed back to Test 1, rent the street can carry.

**The hype cafes** are the small version. Across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Noida, aesthetic cafes open to queues and reels, then go quiet within months ([ThePrint](https://theprint.in/feature/noida-prefers-cafe-culture-restaurants-and-bars-keep-shutting-down/2040122/), 2024). The numbers explain why: about 85 of every 100 first-time guests never return, and only 3 become regulars ([Bloom Intelligence](https://bloomintelligence.com/blog/first-time-restaurant-guests-return-rate/), US data). Hence a cafe that spends its budget on the first visit has nothing left for the second.

### Lessons

The three stories look different, a funded chain, a debt-laden giant and a 40-seat aesthetic cafe, but they broke in the same place. Each grew the number of visits or stores before each visit or store paid for itself. Third Wave survived because it stopped and fixed the store; CCD did not have that option because the debt was already due.

**The alternative path:** open one cafe, run it until it pays its own rent, staff and a small profit for six months, and only then open the second, funded from savings or equity rather than debt. It is slower, but it is the path every survivor in this booklet ended up on, by choice or by force.

chapters.title: Tier-2 cities
chapters.markdown:
A **tier-2 city** here means a fast-growing city below the eight metros, such as Lucknow, Jaipur, Indore, Nagpur, Coimbatore or Patna. The four tests are the same, but the answers change, mostly because of Test 1.

**The rent gap is the whole story.** A 1,000 sq ft cafe on Indiranagar's 100 Feet Road pays about Rs 375 per sq ft a month ([Cushman & Wakefield](https://assets.cushmanwakefield.com/-/media/cw/marketbeat-pdfs/2026/q3/apac-and-gc/bengaluru-retail-q3-2026.pdf?rev=50b06e88da194a1993c7f4776a06ec74), Q3 2026), while a good Lucknow high street was closer to Rs 100 ([Indian Retailer, citing CBRE](https://indianretailer.com/article/retail-business/retail-trends/tier-ii-cities-fast-emerging-growth-frontier-retail-sector), 2022 figures, the latest we could find). To keep rent at 20%, the Indiranagar cafe needs about 179 bills a day at Rs 350; the Lucknow cafe needs about 67 at Rs 250. Hence a tier-2 cafe can survive on a crowd that a metro cafe would call a slow day.

| Same 1,000 sq ft cafe | Indiranagar, Bengaluru | Lucknow high street |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rent a month | Rs 3.75 lakh | Rs 1.00 lakh |
| Average bill (assumption) | Rs 350 | Rs 250 |
| Bills a day to keep rent at 20% | About 179 | About 67 |

### Who is winning there

**Barista** is the chain many had written off. It recently opened its 500th cafe in Patna, adds 50 to 60 outlets a year, expects Rs 400 crore of network sales in FY26 and targets 800 to 900 cafes by about 2030. Its CEO says tier-2 and tier-3 stores are more profitable than metro ones because of lower rents and running costs ([Restaurant India](https://www.restaurantindia.in/news/restaurant-india-news-barista-coffee-targets-800-900-stores-by-2030-eyes-tier-ii-iii-towns-for.n15095), 2026). Thus the brand that lost the metro race found its footing where the rent is lighter.

**Roastery Coffee House** went the other way from the 600 sq ft metro bar. Its cafes are about 5,000 sq ft, with full table service, no takeaway cups and no more than three cafes in any one city, mostly off main streets in residential areas ([Fresh Cup](https://freshcup.com/how-indias-smaller-cities-are-rewriting-the-rules-of-specialty-coffee-expansion/), 2026). e.g. Lucknow and Jaipur both opened on the same day in 2022. Hence in a tier-2 city the big, slow, sit-down cafe is affordable in a way it never is in Bandra.

**Corridor Seven** in Nagpur has not spent on advertising since 2018, and now runs three cafes, five quick-service outlets and a roastery that supplies cafes across India (same source). Its regulars and cupping sessions do the marketing. Thus it is the flywheel from the toolkit, working in a city most founders overlook.

### Who got caught

**Zepto Cafe** paused about 44 outlets in Agra, Chandigarh, Meerut, Mohali and Amritsar in May 2025, affecting more than 400 staff, citing costs and supply chain problems ([Entrackr](https://entrackr.com/news/zepto-cafe-hits-pause-in-smaller-cities-amid-supply-chain-woes-and-high-burn-9299567), 2025). The demand was there; the beans, milk and trained staff did not arrive reliably. Hence a supply chain that works in a metro can break 300 km away.

**The Didi Cafes** in Madhya Pradesh are government-office cafes run by women's self-help groups. In Bhopal, one cafe's daily takings fell from Rs 10,000 to 15,000 to about Rs 1,200 once its main patron, the chief minister, left office ([Free Press Journal](https://www.freepressjournal.in/amp/bhopal/bhopal-didi-cafes-lose-steam-face-losses), 2024). Thus a cafe that depends on one source of footfall, whether a patron or a trend, has no regulars of its own.

The lesson from tier-2 is not that smaller cities are easy. It is that cheaper rent buys a cafe time to build its regulars, as long as the supply chain is built before the second city.

chapters.title: Case Competition Slide Strategy
chapters.markdown:
If this case came up in a competition, we would tell it in three slides. Each slide carries one message, and the headline is the message.

**Slide 1, "Cafes don't run out of guests; they run out of second visits."** We open with the leak: 100 first-time guests, 15 who come back at all, 3 who become regulars. Beside it sits the sum that matters, 825 regulars needed against about 3,000 visits from a launch reel. The judges should see within ten seconds that demand was never the problem.

**Slide 2, "Every big name broke in the same place."** One timeline, three rows: Third Wave (about 70% of stores losing money, then the reset), Cafe Coffee Day (1,752 cafes to 469 under debt) and Tata Starbucks (loss of Rs 135.7 crore, capital paused). One red marker on each row shows the moment growth outran the store. Hence the slide argues a pattern, not three anecdotes.

**Slide 3, "Prove one cafe, then follow the rent."** We close with the recommendation: rent under 20%, a way to capture every first visit, six profitable months before the second cafe, and tier-2 as the next map, with the Indiranagar versus Lucknow bills-a-day comparison as the proof. Thus the deck ends on what to do, not on what went wrong.

The full 10-slide version of this booklet is in the deck that comes with it.

chapters.title: Second Cup Club
chapters.markdown:
**Second Cup Club** (a working name) is a 600 sq ft coffee bar designed around one number, the second visit. Every first-time guest leaves with a card for a free second cup if they come back within 14 days, and the cafe takes a name and a number at the counter so it can remind them. The cost of those free cups sits inside running costs, because it is cheaper than a reel that brings guests who never return.

We model the same cafe on a metro street (Koramangala, Rs 227 per sq ft, [Cushman & Wakefield](https://assets.cushmanwakefield.com/-/media/cw/marketbeat-pdfs/2026/q3/apac-and-gc/bengaluru-retail-q3-2026.pdf?rev=50b06e88da194a1993c7f4776a06ec74)) and on a tier-2 street (Lucknow, Rs 100 per sq ft, CBRE 2022). Cost shares follow the benchmarks in *The cafe owner's toolkit*: cost of goods around 30% and staff around 28% of revenue.

| A month, 600 sq ft | Metro | Tier-2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bills a day x average bill | 77 x Rs 350 | 53 x Rs 250 |
| Revenue | Rs 8.10 lakh | Rs 3.96 lakh |
| Rent | Rs 1.36 lakh (16.8%) | Rs 0.60 lakh (15.2%) |
| Cost of goods (30%) | Rs 2.43 lakh | Rs 1.19 lakh |
| Staff (28%) | Rs 2.27 lakh | Rs 1.11 lakh |
| Other, incl. free second cups | Rs 1.06 lakh | Rs 0.53 lakh |
| **Profit** | **Rs 0.98 lakh (12.1%)** | **Rs 0.53 lakh (13.3%)** |
| Setup cost | Rs 30 lakh | Rs 15 lakh |
| Payback | About 31 months | About 28 months |
| Breakeven | About 64 bills a day | About 43 bills a day |
| Regulars needed (4 visits a month) | About 580 | About 400 |

Two things stand out. First, the tier-2 cafe earns about half the profit but needs half the setup money, so it pays back slightly faster and needs about 180 fewer regulars. Second, both cafes live or die on the regulars line, not the rent line. If the second-cup card brings back about 30% of first-timers, close to the 29.9% that a post-visit thank-you message brought back in [Bloom Intelligence's](https://bloomintelligence.com/blog/restaurant-customer-retention-2026-guide/) benchmarks (2026, US vendor data), and one in five returners becomes a regular, the metro cafe needs about 9,700 first visits instead of the 19,300 it would need at the 3% benchmark. Hence the cheapest marketing in the model is the free second cup.

**What would make us stop:** if after six months the cafe is below breakeven bills a day, or fewer than one in ten first-timers has come back, we fix the cafe before we spend another rupee on it, exactly as Third Wave did.

*Figures are illustrative, built on the sourced benchmarks; bill sizes, bills a day, setup costs and return rates are our assumptions. Tier-2 rent is from 2022 and is likely higher today.*

> Hype buys the first visit. The second cup pays the rent.
